newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Middle East crisis to dominate Euro-Med conference.
newsitem.headline: Middle East crisis to dominate Euro-Med conference.

text.p: Booming economic, cultural and political ties are likely to be overshadowed by the Middle East crisis when the European Union's Foreign Ministers meet 12 of their Mediterranean counterparts in Malta next week.
"Unfortunetely, despite our best intentions, it seems the current situation (in the Middle East) will be ever present," said one senior EU official involved in the meeting.
"But really this meeting is not about the Middle East...it is about the EU's relations with the Mediterranean. The peace process is for another forum," he added.
The Malta meeting on April 15-16 is the second ministerial-level gathering of the so-called Euro-Mediterranean Partnership, launched in Barcelona in 1995.

The EU, attempting to allay fears from Mediterranean countries that its economic interests lay only in eastern Europe, pledged over $6.3 billion in grants, soft loans and development projects between 1995 and 1999.
Much of this has already been gratefully snapped up by the Mediterranean countries and used in projects ranging from re-greening of the desert to establishing pro-democracy groups.

The EU has placed its relations with Mediterranean nations on three pillars -- economic, political and social. All three issues will be tackled separately on Wednesday following Tuesday's opening meeting during which each country will make an individual presentation.
It is this session that organisers fear will be taken over by table-thumping about the Middle East crisis, but officials are nevetheless trying to put a positive spin on it.
"At least the Arab countries and the Israelis will be around the same table," said one official.
The Arab League said last week it was suspending all links with Israel following Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's decision to press ahead with new Jewish settlements in Arab east Jerusalem.
The decision has sparked renewed clashes between Israeli forces and Palestinians, prompted a flurry of international diplomacy and sparked fears for the future of the Oslo peace accords.

While some EU countries, particularly France, have made no secret of their desire for a greater role in the Middle East, others feel the process could best be served by grass-roots democracy and information campaigns to build bridges between Israel and the Arab world.

The EU has earmarked a further $11.2 million this year to supplement the $12.6 million it has already spent on projects promoting human rights in the region, with five percent of this dedicated to promoting harmony between Israelis and Palestinians.

The Malta meeting will also review progress being made on efforts to smoothe trade between the EU and Mediterranean by harmonising customs and standards procedures as well as local certification for exports.
But despite the huge budget the EU has given to relations with the region, most of the 15-nation bloc's more formal relations are governed by bilateral relations with individual countries.

Outstanding association agreements -- which offer lucrative trade priovileges -- are currently being finalised with Tunisia, Morocco and Israel and officials say they hope the Malta meeting may provide an opportunity for progress.
